Decisions needed from you: (1) accept the low open findings or schedule them; (2) who updates register.json after #720 merges (two entries are now out of date); (3) add a post-deploy "delete rbac:version:*" step for migrations that change grants (O-1).

2. What is this, in plain words

A cache is a short-term copy of something that lives in the database, kept so the app does not ask the database every time. Like a sticky note on the fridge with the shopping list: fast to read, wrong if someone changes the real list and forgets to change the note. "Invalidation" is tearing up the note when the list changes. This task checks that every note is torn up, or expires, in the time we promised.

Glossary. TTL: time to live, the seconds a copy may be kept. Stale window: how long an old value can still be served after the source changed. Writer: any code that changes the source (API, worker, CLI, migration). Tombstone: a marker saying "this is revoked". Epoch: a platform-wide number; raising it makes all older login tokens invalid. Two instances: two separate app processes sharing one database and Redis.

3. How we tested

  1. Create a migrated throwaway database and a private Redis (random name, removed at the end). The shared containers are never touched.
  2. Start a second real OS process with the real classes (own memory).
  3. Fill the cache, change the source through the real writer class, read on both processes.
  4. Measure stale seconds on a real clock where a TTL is the only mechanism.
  5. Inject faults: a TCP proxy that refuses connections (lost invalidation), delays held between read and cache fill (set-after-invalidate), 50 parallel readers.
  6. A scanner finds every file that writes a cached source; a unit test fails when one is neither covered nor exempted.

Why it matters, in plain words. D2: after a "revoke all sessions" while Redis blinked, other servers kept accepting old tokens for ever. D4 and D6: a request in flight at the wrong moment could put a suspended person or a removed permission back for 30 s and 600 s. D1: two admins revoking one after the other could revoke nothing. The rest are shorter delays (30 to 60 s).

6. Rollout and rollback

Not a staged rollout. All fixes are small code changes with no data migration; roll back by reverting the commit. D2 adds a 30 s expiry to auth:epoch in Redis: after deploy the key is refilled from Postgres once per 30 s. D4 adds keys auth:gate-gen:* (120 s expiry).

7. What this does NOT prove

  • Not 100% of caches: 9 with a changeable source are not tested (R25, M09, M11, M13, M14, M15, M17, M20, M21); R16 is covered by the scanner only.
  • In-process caches of P1 services were tested with a second instance in the same process (an in-process cache cannot tell the difference); the two-real-process proof covers settings, epoch, halt, gate, RBAC, suspension, partner flag, sessions, impersonation, plans.
  • The full HTTP stack (guards, controllers) was not booted; real service classes were driven directly. Guards that read the same keys were checked by reading the keys.
  • The 600 s Redis TTLs (RBAC version, operator permissions) were not waited out: the TTL was read from Redis and the expiry brought forward with EXPIRE. The measured 30, 60 s waits are real.
  • Writers in other repositories, web and mobile apps, the client-side query cache (C01-C03) and HTTP/CDN caches were not tested.
  • The scanner reads source text: a table name built at run time would be invisible. It also over-matches (a column name near a statement), which is why some entries are exempt with that reason.
  • Writers marked "TTL only" were not individually reproduced unless listed in the appendix.
  • Not run against production data, a cluster Redis, or Sentinel failover.
  • Migrations that change grants leave up to 600 s of stale grant sets: documented, not fixed (O-1).
